Saving every month through 67 years of the S&P/TSX: how often the account sat below what was paid in

Monthly contributions from pay are often described as a cure for bad timing. Using Statistics Canada’s monthly S&P/TSX Composite closes from 1956 to 2023, follow the same monthly saving plan from every starting month: how it ended, how long it spent below the money paid in, how inflation changes the answer, and when phasing in a lump sum helped.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 27 October 2026 · 7 min read
Sources reviewed 27 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Saving $500 at every month-end for 10 years, in an index fund that followed the S&P/TSX Composite price plus a 2.5% yield less a 0.5% fee, the median start ended with 1.48 dollars per dollar paid in across 693 starting months from 1956-01 to 2013-09. 0.4% of starts ended below the money paid in, and 11.3% below it once each contribution is raised by the CPI. The worst start, 1964-12, ended at 0.96. For a lump sum already saved, investing at once beat a 12-month phase-in for 63% of starts, with a median difference of 3.0%. The index is real; the yield, fee and cash rate are your assumptions; months overlap and the record is one market's past.

The central idea

Saving CAD 500 a month for ten years in a fund that followed the S&P/TSX Composite price plus an assumed 2.5% yield less a 0.5% fee, the median of 693 starting months from 1956 to 2013 ended with CAD 1.48 for every dollar paid in, the worst (December 1964) with CAD 0.96. Only 3 of 693 starts ended below the money paid in, but 11% ended below it once each contribution is raised by the CPI, and the typical plan still spent a tenth of its months under water, up to 35 months in a row. Over five years, a monthly saver ended below the money paid in more often (6.9%) than a lump sum invested at once (4.8%). For money already saved, investing at once beat a 12-month phase-in for 63% of starts. This is one market’s past with assumed dividends and fees, not a forecast.

01

What a monthly plan actually protects against

Investing the same amount from every paycheque is usually called dollar-cost averaging. Its appeal is that nobody has to pick a moment: some contributions buy near a peak, some in a fall and the rest in between. But “spread out” is not the same as “safe”. A monthly saver can still end a plan with less than was paid in, can spend long stretches watching the balance sit below the total deposited, and can lose purchasing power even when the dollar figure looks fine.

This guide follows one simple plan from every possible starting month in Statistics Canada’s S&P/TSX Composite series, January 1956 to September 2023: a fixed amount at each month-end, for a set number of years, in a fund that tracked the index price plus a constant dividend yield less a fee. It then separates the paycheque question from a different one: what to do with a lump sum that is already saved. The record-high guide uses the same data to look at single purchases.

02

How the same plan ended, depending only on when it started

The first chart plots, for every starting month, what the account was worth at the end as a share of the money paid in. With CAD 500 a month for ten years (CAD 60,000 in total), a 2.5% yield and a 0.5% fee, the median start ended at 147.7%, or CAD 1.48 per dollar and about CAD 88,600 in all. The best start, August 1990, ended at CAD 2.70 per dollar, carried by the late-1990s rise. The worst, December 1964, ended at CAD 0.96: its last contributions went in during the 1973–74 fall, and the plan finished in December 1974 near the bottom.

The width of that range is the main lesson. Nothing about the saver’s habits differed between those starts; only the calendar did. A plan’s result depends heavily on what the market does in its last few years, when most of the money is already in. That is why a monthly plan with a fixed end date, such as a home purchase in ten years, carries more timing risk at the end than at the start. The return-order guide shows the same effect with authored returns.

03

Inside the worst start: value against money paid in

The second chart follows the worst starting month for the period you choose. For ten years that is December 1964: the account was below the money paid in at 20 of its 120 month-ends and ended CAD 2,235 short. Raised by the CPI to December 1974 prices, the CAD 60,000 paid in was worth about CAD 83,000, so the shortfall in purchasing power was far larger than the dollar shortfall.

Choose five years and the worst start becomes February 2004, ending in February 2009 at CAD 0.78 per dollar after the global financial crisis. The longest unbroken stretch below the money paid in for any ten-year plan was 35 months, for plans that began around the 2000 peak: a saver who started in June 2000 watched the balance sit under the total deposited for almost three years and still ended at CAD 1.34 per dollar, helped by the low prices paid during the fall. Living through those months is the real test of a monthly plan, and the keep-or-pause guide shows what stopping contributions in a fall would have cost.

04

Below the money paid in, and below its purchasing power

The third chart counts how many starting months ended below the money put in, for holding periods from five to thirty years. For a monthly saver over ten years, it was 3 of 693 starts (0.4%). But raise each contribution by the CPI to the final month, which asks whether the account at least kept what the savings could buy, and 78 starts (11%) fell short; 72 of them began in the 1960s or 1970s and ended in the high-inflation years that followed. Over twenty years 6% fell short in real terms, and over thirty years none did.

The third bar is a lump sum invested at the start and held for the same period. Over five years it ended below its amount for 4.8% of starts, less often than the monthly saver’s 6.9%, because a lump sum spends its whole period in the market while the saver’s later contributions have only months to recover from a fall. Dollar-cost averaging reduces the chance of putting everything in at the worst moment; it does not, by itself, reduce the chance of ending a short plan behind. The inflation-window guide shows how much the price level moved in each of those spans.

05

Money already saved is a different decision

A paycheque contribution cannot be invested before it is earned, so for monthly saving there is nothing to phase in. A lump sum already in the bank—an inheritance, a bonus, a home sale—is different: it can go in at once or in equal parts over several months, with the waiting part earning interest. The heatmap compares the two for CAD 60,000 over ten years, by how far the index stood below its previous peak at the start.

With a 3% cash rate, investing at once beat a 12-month phase-in for 63% of starting months, by a median of 3.0% of the final value. When the index was more than 20% below its peak, investing at once won 72% of the time; at a record close the share fell to between 49% and 63% depending on the phase-in length. Phasing in helped most for the starts just before the deepest falls: from June 2000 a 12-month phase-in ended about 13% ahead. Those starts could not be identified in advance. The phased investing guide lays out the regret-versus-expected-return trade-off with authored returns.

06

Fund, account and tax: separate questions

The index fund in this guide is an assumption, and so is the account. Inside a TFSA, the Canada Revenue Agency says income from interest, dividends or capital gains is generally tax-free, even when withdrawn, though contributions are not deductible. In an RRSP, contributions are deductible and withdrawals are taxed as income. In a taxable account, the fund’s distributions are taxed each year and selling can create a capital gain. The fund itself is not tax-exempt anywhere; the account’s rules decide the tax. A monthly plan that fits inside the available room avoids the question for that money, and the TFSA timing guide compares a January deposit with contributions from each paycheque.

Many savers use a balanced fund rather than an all-equity index fund. With bonds beside stocks, a balanced fund has usually fallen less in equity crashes, which shortens the months below the money paid in, though it has also tended to grow less over long periods and did fall with stocks in 2022. The balanced fund guide works through that trade-off.

07

What this history can and cannot tell you

  • Starting months overlap heavily: two ten-year plans a month apart share 119 of their 120 months, so 693 starts are far fewer independent outcomes.
  • The index is a price index that leaves out dividends. The constant yield you choose stands in for them; actual dividend yields on Canadian stocks varied widely and were often higher before 2000.
  • The series covers one market, concentrated in financial, energy and materials companies, and ends in September 2023, so later years are not included.
  • Fees, taxes, currency exposure and the fund’s actual holdings change real results. A higher fee lowers every outcome.
  • Contributions here never pause, never rise with pay and are never withdrawn early; real plans often do all three.
  • Nothing here predicts future returns or recommends buying, selling or holding any investment.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 27 October 2026. Every chart applies the actual monthly price changes of the S&P/TSX Composite Index from Statistics Canada table 10-10-0125-01 (vector v122620, 813 month-end closes from January 1956 to September 2023, retrieved through the Web Data Service on 27 October 2026). The CPI comparison uses table 18-10-0004-01 (vector v41690973) for the same months. The dividend yield, fund fee, monthly amount, lump sum and cash rate are your assumptions and are held constant; they are not history. Nothing here forecasts the index or any fund.
